 Abstract 
 Large Language Models (LLMs) often exhibit increased response latency and degraded answer quality as dialogue length grows, making effective context management essential. However, existing methods rely on extra LLM calls to build memory or perform offline memory construction without considering the current user utterance, which can introduce inefficiencies or disrupt conversational continuity. We introduce DyCP , a lightweight context management method that dynamically segment and retrieve relevant memory at query time. It preserves the sequential structure of dialogue without predefined topic boundaries and supports efficient, adaptive context retrieval. Across three long-form dialogue benchmarks— LoCoMo , MT-Bench+ , and SCM4LLMs —and multiple LLMs, DyCP consistently improves answer quality while reducing response latency. We also examine the gap between modern LLMs’ expanded context windows and their actual long-context processing capacity, highlighting the continued importance of effective context management. 
 1 Introduction 
 Large Language Models (LLMs)-powered dialogue systems support long-form, open-domain conversations that span hundreds of turns with frequent topic shifts. To preserve contextual coherence, these systems typically prepend the entire dialogue history to each new user utterance. While this approach helps maintain continuity, it introduces growing overhead. Longer inputs increase inference costs—whether in GPU resources or API usage—and slow down response latency. As the context expands, the model also faces a needle-in-a-haystack problem Kamradt (2023) , where identifying relevant information (the needle ) becomes difficult, as key details are often buried in the surrounding dialogue (the haystack ). 
 To mitigate these issues, prior work—alongside efforts to improve the long-context handling capabilities of LLMs—has explored external context management strategies such as summarization  ( Wang et al., 2025b ; LangChain Team, 2023 ) and retrieval-based selection of past turns, either at the turn level  ( Maharana et al., 2024 ) or segment level  ( Pan et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2023 ) . However, summarization may omit key details necessary for the current turn. Turn-level retrieval can be query-targeted and efficient, but can disrupt coherence by ignoring discourse continuity and structural dependencies. Segment-level retrieval better preserves context by grouping related turns into topic-level segments, but existing methods assume fixed topic boundaries based on pre-segmentation. In practice, however, these boundaries may vary with the current user utterance, suggesting that segmentation should instead be query-dependent. 
 Figure 1 : For the current user utterance (Turn 96), which requests the RTG3 task defined earlier in the conversation, the agent generates terms like bank and a handful of coins when using the pruned context selected by our method (Turns 7–15), accurately reflecting the task intent. In contrast, using the full context (Turns 1–95) results in outputs like library and book , which are plausible but slightly off-topic for the [bank] and [money] theme. While this example uses top-1 pruning, our method generally selects multiple segments dynamically. Pruning also reduces first-token latency about three times in this example. 
 This paper introduces DyCP , a dynamic context pruning method that selects coherent context segments at query time without relying on pre-segmentation. Given a user query, our method computes its relevance to previous dialogue turns and identifies a sequence of contiguous spans with sustained relevance using KadaneDial , our extension of Kadane’s algorithm  1 1 
 1 
 The original Kadane’s algorithm  Bentley (1984) is a classic linear-time method to find the maximum subarray. . It preserves the relevant context while significantly reducing the input length. Figure  1 illustrates our method in action. To illustrate long-context behavior, we run GPT-4o  2 2 
 2 
 https://platform.openai.com/docs/models/gpt-4o on a 96-turn conversation from the SCM4LLMs dataset  Wang et al. (2025a) . With only 9 turns of pruned context, GPT-4o generates a response that is not only faster but also more accurate than one generated using the full context. 
 In this work, we examine how DyCP differs from existing methods through empirical analysis and discuss the relationship between modern LLMs’ expanded context windows, their actual long-context processing capacity, and the role of context management methods such as DyCP . We conduct experiments on three long-form dialogue benchmarks and compare DyCP with six alternative approaches using both closed- and open-source LLMs that support chat-style interaction and long context windows of at least 128k tokens. In summary, our contributions are as follows: 
 • 
 We propose a dynamic context management method that selects coherent, query-relevant segments from earlier dialogue in real time, without pre-segmentation (Section  4 ). 
 • 
 We comprehensively evaluate our method against six other methods on three benchmarks, using a diverse set of LLMs to assess robustness across models (Section  5 ). 
 • 
 We analyze how factors—dialogue length, relevant-context position, and retrieval recall—affect context-management effectiveness in modern LLMs, providing practical guidance for method design (Section  6 ). 
 2 Related Work 
 LLMs’ Long - Context Handling Capacity   Recent LLMs have improved their ability to process long input sequences through advancements in both training and inference techniques. Chen et al. (2023) propose a fine-tuning method that extends the model’s positional encoding to support longer contexts while preserving original performance. Building on this, Peng et al. (2024) enhance fine-tuning efficiency, enabling models to handle up to 128k tokens with significantly less training. Furthermore, An et al. (2024a) introduce an inference-time approach that chunks the input text and links the segments, allowing long-context processing without any additional training. 
 External Context Management Methods   Parallel to architectural advances, other work focuses on managing long context outside the model. To evaluate context management in long-form open-domain conversations, Maharana et al. (2024) introduces the LoCoMo benchmark and shows that turn-level retrieval produces better responses than feeding the entire dialogue history to LLMs. Lu et al. (2023) presents the MT-Bench+ benchmark and proposes MemoChat , a segment-level retrieval approach that leverages LLMs for both segmentation and retrieval. Pan et al. (2025) demonstrates that segment-level retrieval outperforms turn-level and session-level methods, and presents SeCom , which combines LLM-based segmentation, lightweight retrieval, and context denoising. Wang et al. (2025a) releases the SCM4LLMs benchmark and introduces a turn-level retrieval mechanism composed of multiple LLM-based agents, including memory summarization and memory controller modules. 
 3 Our Contribution 
 Our method requires only minimal LLM calls overall, avoiding offline segmentation based on fixed topic boundaries as done in prior segment-level approaches. It performs dynamic segmentation and retrieval at query time, enabling efficient and adaptive context retrieval. 
 4 Method 
 This section describes how DyCP dynamically manages context in long-form dialogue. Given the current user question ( q n q_{n} ), the dialogue history 𝐇 \mathbf{H} contains the preceding n − 1 n{-}1 turns, where each turn is an utterance pair ( q k , a k ) (q_{k},a_{k}) . We treat turns independently: each pair is concatenated into a single text unit and encoded by the bi-encoder  3 3 
 3 
 A bi-encoder encodes the input and candidate items independently with shared parameters, allowing efficient embedding-based retrieval  Lei et al. (2023) . retriever ( B ) separately for each turn. Thus, embeddings are computed on a per-turn basis, and the resulting sequence of embeddings is stored as:

\mathbf{H}^{\text{emb}}=[\texttt{B}(h_{1}),\texttt{B}(h_{2}),\ldots,\texttt{B}(h_{n{-}1})]\in\mathbb{R}^{(n-1)\times d}\end{split} 
 At the current turn, only the new user query q n q_{n} is encoded into an embedding q n emb q_{n}^{\text{emb}} . This embedding is compared against the pre-computed turn-level history embeddings 𝐇 emb \mathbf{H}^{\text{emb}} to obtain a relevance-score sequence 𝐒 \mathbf{S} . Using 𝐒 \mathbf{S} , our extended Kadane algorithm KadaneDial (Algorithm  1 ) identifies one or more contiguous spans in the dialogue history whose cumulative relevance remains consistently high—for example, ( h s 1 : e 1 ) , ( h s 2 : e 2 ) , ( h s 3 : e 3 ) (h_{s_{1}{:}e_{1}}),(h_{s_{2}{:}e_{2}}),(h_{s_{3}{:}e_{3}}) , where each span corresponds to a slice of consecutive turns. These spans are then concatenated in their original chronological order to form the pruned history ℋ ′ = [ h s 1 , … , h e 1 , … , h s 3 , … , h e 3 ] \mathcal{H}^{\prime}=[h_{s_{1}},\dots,h_{e_{1}},\dots,h_{s_{3}},\dots,h_{e_{3}}] . This continuity-preserving sequence ℋ ′ \mathcal{H}^{\prime} is given to the agent (typically an LLM) together with the current q n q_{n} as:

\mathbf{S}&=\mathbf{H}^{\text{emb}}\cdot{q_{n}}^{\text{emb}}\in\mathbb{R}^{(n{-}1)\times 1}\\
\mathcal{H}^{\prime}&=\texttt{KadaneDial}(\mathbf{S})\\
a_{n}&=\texttt{LLM}([\mathcal{H}^{\prime};\,q_{n}])\end{split} 
 We extend the classic Kadane’s algorithm ( L7 to L14 ) in KadaneDial to identify salient context segments in long-form dialogue. The relevance sequence 𝐒 \mathbf{S} is reinterpreted as a one-dimensional signal, where contiguous high-scoring regions indicate discourse segments that are locally coherent and relevant to the current turn. To account for variation in score distributions across queries and dialogues, we apply z-score normalization and subtract a gain threshold  τ \tau to center the signal ( L1 to L4 ). It then iteratively identifies all sub-optimal spans whose cumulative gain 𝔾 \mathbb{G} (i.e., the score sum of the best segment in each iteration) exceeds a stopping threshold  θ \theta . This design reflects a conservative strategy that prioritizes recall—favoring the inclusion of borderline-relevant context over the risk of omitting critical segments—while preserving the sequential nature of dialogue.

 5.2 Models 
 We evaluate DyCP against six methods, as follows: No Context , Full Context , MemoChat , SCM4LLMs , SeCom and CondMem . 
 • 
 No Context runs without any dialogue history, serving as a lower-bound reference. 
 • 
 Full Context prepends the entire dialogue history to the input, offering a comparison point without any context management. 
 • 
 SCM4LLMs Wang et al. (2025a) employs multiple LLM-based agents, such as memory summarization and control, in a turn-level retrieval framework. 
 • 
 MemoChat Lu et al. (2023) manages segment-level dialogue context, using LLMs to perform both segmentation and retrieval. 
 • 
 SeCom Pan et al. (2025) refines dialogue context through LLM-based segmentation, dense retrieval, and context denoising to construct compact contexts. 
 • 
 CondMem Yuan et al. (2025) builds hybrid memory representations by combining summarization-based dialogue compression with selective memory construction. 
 The main experiments were conducted using three conversational agents via API access: GPT-4o, Claude 3.7 (Sonnet), and GPT-4o mini. GPT-4o and Claude 3.7 are comparable models from different providers, while GPT-4o mini is a smaller variant of GPT-4o that offers moderate performance with the same input context limit. In addition, we include two recently released models—GPT-4.1 and Claude 4.0—to assess improvements in long-context understanding and to examine whether our method remains effective. Table  2 summarizes the per-million-token input and output costs for all API models used. In addition, we evaluate whether DyCP generalizes to open-source conversational models.  5.2.1 Growth of LLM Context Windows 
 Modern LLMs have steadily expanded their context limits over successive generations. As shown in Figure  2 , GPT models have grown from about 1K tokens in GPT-2 to up to 1M tokens in recent GPT-4 models. However, prior experiments such as MemoChat , SCM4LLMs , and SeCom were constrained to GPT-3.5–Turbo–level models (4k tokens), which cannot ingest the full dialogue history of long-form benchmarks—for example, even one-third of a single LoCoMo dialogue exceeds this limit. Thus, any Full Context baseline in those settings would have required truncation. Although CondMem uses GPT-4 for memory construction, it was not evaluated on publicly released long-form dialogue benchmarks, and its Full Context behavior remains unclear. In contrast, we conduct comparative experiments using modern models that support at least 128k tokens, enabling the entire dialogue history of all benchmarks to be included without truncation and allowing a direct comparison between long-context LLMs and context-management methods. 
 Figure 2 : Input context limits (in tokens) of GPT APIs, ranging from GPT-2 to GPT-4 series. 
 5.2.2 Computational Cost Analysis 
 As shown in Table  3 , the methods differ in both the number of LLM calls they require and the size of each call’s input. Regarding offline costs, MemoChat , SeCom and CondMem all require LLM calls that take all previous turns (AT) as input when constructing memory, so their designs appear similar at a high level. However, their practical preprocessing cost differs significantly in our benchmarks, where the full dialogue prior to test queries is already available. MemoChat and SeCom require only a single O ⁡ ( 1 × | A ​ T | ) O(1\times|AT|) pass over the dialogue during preprocessing. In contrast, CondMem constructs memory cumulatively—each step reprocesses the entire dialogue so far, and the resulting memory is fed into the next step. This chain of interdependent updates leads to O ⁡ ( n × | A ​ T | ) O(n\times|AT|) preprocessing calls, making API-based evaluation infeasible; thus, we evaluate CondMem only with open-source models (see Section 5.6 ). SCM4LLMs also performs turn-level preprocessing but do one turn at a time, avoiding repeated full-history calls and remaining substantially cheaper than CondMem . Finally, DyCP performs no offline calls and is therefore highly efficient. In terms of online cost, SeCom and DyCP are the most efficient methods, each requiring only a single M+Q call per query, while others add memory control or retrieval calls during inference.

 5.2.3 Retriever 
 As DyCP , SCM4LLMs , SeCom and CondMem include a retriever component in their frameworks, we experiment with four different retrievers, including variants of Contriever  Izacard et al. (2021) and BGE  Chen et al. (2024) , as presented in Table  5 (Section  5.5 ). We use facebook/contriever-msmarco 7 7 
 7 
 https://huggingface.co/facebook/contriever-msmarco for downstream answer generation across all methods, as it consistently shows the best performance. Note that CondMem produces and retrieves memory chunks that do not preserve turn boundaries, making turn-level gold comparison infeasible. 
 5.3 Evaluation Metrics 
 We evaluate context management methods using three metrics: Answer Quality, Response Latency, and Retrieval Accuracy. 
 Answer Quality   We adopt GPT4Score, following prior work  Lu et al. (2023) ; Pan et al. (2025) ; Yuan et al. (2025) , in which GPT-4 serves as a judge and assigns a score from 1 to 100 based on how well the model response answers the user question. This aligns our evaluation with common practice and provides consistent, scalable assessments. The evaluation prompt (Figure  3 ) provides GPT-4 with the conversation history, user question, model response, and gold answer as input. 
 Evaluation Prompt 
 You are an impartial judge. You will be shown Conversation History, User Question, Gold Response and Bot Response. 
 Conversation History: 
 {{ conversation_history }} 
 User Question: 
 {{ current_user_question }} 
 Gold Response: 
 {{ gold_answer }} 
 Bot Response: 
 {{ model_response }} 
 Please evaluate whether the Bot Response accurately answers the User Question, referencing the appropriate information from the long Conversation History, and using the Gold Response as a reference. Begin your evaluation by providing a short explanation, then you must rate Bot Response on an integer rating of 1 to 100 by strictly following this format: [[rating]]. 
 Figure 3: Evaluation prompt used in GPT4Score 
 To verify that GPT4Score aligns with human judgment, we also conduct a human evaluation on a small subset of samples (Section  5.5.2 ). For the LoCoMo benchmark, which contains short, factual gold answers, we further report Exact Match (EM) and ROUGE  Lin (2004) . For EM, we consider a prediction correct if the model response contains the gold answer string. ROUGE is computed based on n-gram overlap between the model response and the gold answer. These metrics are omitted for other benchmarks due to the length and verbosity of their gold answers, which limits the reliability of traditional lexical matching. 
 Response Latency   We measure online first-token latency—the time from receiving the user utterance to generating the first token of the model response—to quantify the additional latency introduced by each memory management method. To observe when the first token is generated, we call all LLMs in streaming mode. 
 Retrieval Accuracy   We use Hit@k, Recall@k, and Precision@k to evaluate how accurately each method retrieves the context relevant to the current turn. As only LoCoMo benchmark provides ground-truth annotations of relevant context for each test question, we use LoCoMo for this evaluation. Each metric is defined as follows: 
 • 
 Hit@k indicates whether any gold context appears in the top-k results. 
 • 
 Recall@k is the proportion of gold contexts covered by the top-k results. 
 • 
 Precision@k is the proportion of the top-k results that include gold context. 
 5.4 Experimental Details 
 For the implementation of DyCP , we set the gain threshold τ \tau to 0.6 and the stopping threshold θ \theta to 1.0 as hyperparameters of the KadaneDial . These values were chosen based on preliminary qualitative inspection of retrieved context spans and were found to produce stable pruning behavior. Because the relevance scores are z-score normalized before span selection, the thresholds operate on a standardized scale. As a result, DyCP is not overly sensitive to the specific numerical choices of τ \tau and θ \theta , and we therefore use the same configuration across all datasets. 
 To ensure a fair comparison in retrieval-based baselines, we match the total number of retrieved turns across methods wherever applicable. For segment-level approaches such as SeCom , we align their retrieval volume with that of DyCP by matching the product of TpS and RS reported in Table  8 . Concretely, this corresponds to retrieving the top 5 turns on LoCoMo , 2 on SCM4LLMs , and 3 on MT-Bench+ . MemoChat performs automatic segment retrieval and therefore does not require specifying a fixed k k . For turn-level retrievers such as SCM4LLMs and CondMem , we follow the original papers and use k = 5 k{=}5 and k = 3 k{=}3 , respectively, for all benchmarks. In all methods, retrieved items are reordered chronologically (i.e., according to their original dialogue order) before being provided to the conversational agent. 
 All experiments with API-based LLMs were conducted using a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU to run retriever, while experiments involving open-source LLMs were run locally on four NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs.

 5.5.1 Answer Quality & Response Latency 
 We evaluate our method on three long-form benchmarks using five conversational agents, including two standard models (GPT-4o, Claude 3.7), a lightweight variant (GPT-4o mini), and two recently released models (GPT-4.1, Claude 4.0). 
 As shown in Table  4 , DyCP consistently achieves the highest answer quality across benchmarks and conversational agents, while maintaining low response latency. Overall, performance generally follows the order: DyCP > Full Context > SeCom > SCM4LLMs > MemoChat , with both DyCP and SeCom distinguished by their low latency. Note that, as discussed in Section  5.2.1 , prior studies used short-context LLMs (e.g., 4k-token models), where the Full Context baseline might have required truncation. In contrast, our setting uses long-context LLMs that can ingest the entire dialogue history, which naturally shifts the relative performance of the baselines. 
 The latency advantages of DyCP directly follow from the computational cost analysis in Section  5.2.2 . Unlike other methods that introduce additional LLM calls during memory construction, control, or retrieval refinement, DyCP performs no extra LLM calls—neither offline nor at query time. This eliminates the overhead of repeatedly reprocessing the dialogue and avoids the variance introduced by multi-stage pipelines. Consequently, the low and stable latency observed across all agents reflects a structural property of the method: DyCP both minimizes the number of LLM calls and reduces the size of each call’s input, enabling efficient inference even for dialogues with hundreds of turns. 
 Figure  4 further illustrates the quality–latency trade-off: our method dominates the upper left quadrant, achieving both high quality and low latency. The performance gap is particularly pronounced on LoCoMo , the longest conversations in terms of turns, highlighting its strength in handling extended dialogue history. The novelty of our method lies in how it departs from the existing segmentation and retrieval paradigms. Rather than relying on pre-segmentation or fixed top-k retrieval, DyCP dynamically identifies the context needed for the current turn in a single pass. This enables flexible, structure-aware context selection that captures coherent discourse units. We provide a more detailed discussion in Section  5.5.3 . 
 For the smaller GPT-4o mini model, performance decreases proportionally while latency is reduced compared to GPT-4o, though the overall trend remains consistent. For the most recent models, GPT-4.1 and Claude 4.0, we observe improved long-context understanding relative to their previous versions. In particular, GPT-4.1 shows a substantial gain over GPT-4o: on LoCoMo , EM increases from 24.23 to 33.67 and GPT4Score rises from 75.13 to 92.06. Under GPT-4.1, the Full Context condition even achieves performance comparable to that of DyCP , and although it attains slightly higher scores in some cases, none of these differences are statistically significant. Meanwhile, DyCP runs more than twice as fast (0.97s vs. 2.41s) and requires far fewer input tokens (Table  6 ). These findings highlight that although LLMs are improving in long-context understanding and now support million-token inputs, feeding the entire context remains inefficient.

 5.5.2 Human Evaluation 
 To validate whether GPT4Score aligns with human judgments, one of the authors conducted a separate evaluation on one LoCoMo dialogue (50 test QA pairs) for responses generated by all six methods: No Context , Full Context , DyCP , Secom , MemoChat , and SCM4LLMs . For each test question, the annotator was shown the user query, the gold answer, and the model-generated answer, with the method identity hidden, and assigned a correctness label from − 1 , 0 , 1 {-1,0,1} , where − 1 -1 indicates an incorrect answer, 0 0 a partially correct answer  8 8 
 8 
 As an example of a partially correct response, when the test query is ”When did Caroline join a mentorship program?” and the gold answer is ”The weekend before 17 July 2023” , the model responded with ”around July 17, 2023” , capturing the rough time period but missing the exact reference. , and 1 1 a correct answer. As shown in Figure  5 , GPT4Score shows consistent differences in distributions across the three human labels and exhibits strong correlations with the human judgments across all methods ( r = 0.417 r=0.417 – 0.842 0.842 , p < 0.01 p<0.01 ), confirming that it provides a reliable approximation of human evaluation.
